contributions.item_title_en: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Transport: Climate Adaptation and Resilience in Wales's Transport Network
contributions.text_english: Today, I am providing an update on the resilience of Wales's transport network and the action that is being taken by the Welsh Government, Transport for Wales and our partners in order to prepare for a changing climate. Reducing carbon emissions remains very important to us. But, in addition to that, we need to prepare for the impacts of climate change, which are already being felt by communities across Wales. People rightly expect transport services to be there when they need them. That is why making sure that our network is reliable and ready to cope with extreme events is such an important responsibility.

Mae lleihau allyriadau carbon yn parhau i fod yn bwysig iawn i ni. Ond, yn ogystal â hynny, mae angen i ni baratoi ar gyfer effeithiau newid hinsawdd, sydd eisoes yn cael eu teimlo gan gymunedau ledled Cymru. Mae pobl yn disgwyl i wasanaethau trafnidiaeth fod ar gael pan fydd eu hangen. Dyna pam mae gwneud yn siŵr bod ein rhwydwaith yn ddibynadwy ac yn gallu ymdopi â digwyddiadau eithafol yn gyfrifoldeb pwysig iawn.

contributions.item_title_en: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Transport: Climate Adaptation and Resilience in Wales's Transport Network
contributions.text_english:
The weather conditions—[Interruption.] Diolch. I appreciate that. The weather conditions experienced across Wales this year have demonstrated how rapidly climate risks are changing. Wales has faced prolonged rainfall, drought, extreme heat and significant wildfire incidents. These are not simply environmental issues, they are transport issues too. These events have reinforced the need to adapt our transport networks so that they can continue to operate safely and reliably in a changing climate.

Later this month, the First Minister will convene a wildfire summit, bringing together the public and private sectors and trade unions to identify ways to reduce the risk of wildfires and make sure we are better prepared to respond when they occur. Extreme heat and wildfires have placed exceptional pressure on infrastructure, services, passengers and staff. I recognise the work of transport organisations, emergency services, local authorities, trade unions and other partners in maintaining safe travel and protecting critical links.

Through my engagement with operators and trade unions, I have heard first-hand the impact that extreme heat, wildfire risk and other severe weather events can have on front-line staff. Their safety and well-being must come first. We will work with Transport for Wales and trade unions to make sure the experience of front-line workers informs the practical measures we put in place. Transport employers must plan for these risks, working with trade unions to identify measures that protect staff and support the safe operation of services.

The challenges experienced across the network this summer demonstrated why this preparation is increasingly important. On the rail network, high temperatures required some trains to be withdrawn because of cooling-system problems. Infrastructure operated close to—and, at times, beyond—historic design limits, leading to speed restrictions and additional failures. But this is not just a rail issue.

contributions.item_title_en: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Transport: Climate Adaptation and Resilience in Wales's Transport Network
contributions.text_english:
Although the most visible impacts this summer were on rail, resilience matters across every mode. Extreme temperatures affected bus services, while flooding, landslips and heat are placing growing pressure on roads and active travel infrastructure. The same principle applies to the international gateways on which Wales depends for connectivity, trade and economic activity.

Our major ferry ports—Holyhead, Fishguard and Pembroke Dock—provide vital international connections for people and goods. The prolonged disruption at Holyhead in December 2024 demonstrated how important our ports are to communities, businesses and the wider Welsh economy. It also showed how quickly disruption at one strategic gateway can have wider consequences. The Irish sea taskforce was established in response, to consider how a similar incident could be avoided and how partners should respond if one occurred at any Welsh port. I intend to publish a six-month update on its recommendations this autumn.

Investment is also strengthening port resilience. Stena Line has committed significant investment in infrastructure at Holyhead and Fishguard to improve resilience, connectivity and future capacity. During my recent visit to Ireland, I met Minister Canney and key stakeholders to discuss resilience and co-operation across these vital routes. I have also asked officials to prepare a joint exercise based on the scenario of an unforeseen Welsh port closure.

These lessons about preparedness, co-ordination and contingency planning apply to other strategic gateways. Cardiff Airport maintains emergency planning arrangements for incidents including severe weather and winter storms. Across aviation and ports, preparedness depends on clear responsibilities, tested plans, and effective communication. Strong partnerships are equally important across the wider network. My officials have established the Wales transport adaptation working group, bringing together infrastructure managers, operators and key stakeholders to support a co-ordinated approach.

I have asked Transport for Wales to take immediate steps to improve resilience to weather conditions that can no longer be treated as exceptional. In the short term, this includes strengthening maintenance and inspection regimes, working to improve the reliability of train cooling systems and taking practical measures to reduce heat impacts on rolling stock. Enhanced weather monitoring, clearer escalation arrangements and pre-planned operational responses will improve preparedness and help reduce disruption during periods of severe weather. The aim is simple: to act earlier, reduce disruption and keep people moving safely.

Alongside these immediate measures, Transport for Wales is developing a longer term adaptation programme. This will embed resilience in the way transport services are planned, operated and invested in for the future. Transport for Wales will work closely with Network Rail, which operates much of the rail infrastructure in Wales, so that plans cover the whole network. Priorities will include better climate-risk information, stronger drainage and earthworks, resilient rail and bus specifications, new monitoring technology, and nature-based solutions. The work will also support the wider cross-Government approach to climate adaptation and resilience that will be reflected through the forthcoming climate and nature action plan.

On the strategic road network, lessons from recent storms, floods and heatwaves are shaping how we manage and maintain our roads, helping us become better prepared for future disruption. We're also working with local authorities to strengthen the wider highway network and rolling out resilience and adaptation training across all 22 authorities. As we move into winter, preparations reflect the growing risks of heavy rainfall, flooding, landslips, storms and coastal impacts, alongside projections for warmer, wetter winters and more intense rainfall. The central lesson is clear: resilience is not simply about maintaining assets; it is about enabling people to travel safely and reliably.

We cannot limit ourselves to responding to today's incidents. We must prepare for the climate of the decades ahead while continuing to reduce emissions. Working with our partners, the Welsh Government is taking practical actions to build a transport system that can withstand future pressures and continue to serve the people of Wales. We cannot prevent every disruption caused by extreme weather, but we can be better prepared, more resilient and more responsive. We can identify risks earlier, act faster when disruption happens, and make sure our network is built and maintained to withstand the conditions we know are coming.

contributions.item_title_en: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Transport: Climate Adaptation and Resilience in Wales's Transport Network
contributions.text_english:
I'm really pleased that Reform is starting to recognise that the climate is starting to cause us real problems on our transport network, because, ultimately, what we're dealing with is the result of years of not addressing the climate issues carefully and properly.

On railways, Transport for Wales I think have managed to see the last—. We had five heatwaves, as we all know, during the summer, and those caused a huge amount of pressure on the Transport for Wales operations. What we noticed is that each time those operations were affected, the resilience was better, because it's not just about dealing with the consequences of that particular action, it's about making sure you improve, and that they improve time and time again. On your point about their service delivery, they've just appeared top of the tree when it comes to services in the most recent period, and I think that bears testament to the work that they're doing, particularly on the core Valleys lines.

Specific improvements related to air conditioning—I think that's a really good point. The air conditioning needs to work for passengers and needs to work for the people who are working on the trains as well. We're carrying on with the investment in the rolling stock to make sure we've got the trains that are suitable for the future. We've still got old stock on our railways. They're going to be taken off those railways as we move forward. But a point that I made a few weeks ago in the Siambr about us being responsible for all of our rail network would enable us to do these things quicker, which at the moment your party doesn't support. I too was next to the Minister for rural resilience talking about flooding earlier, and I think the issues—. He made reference to transport, and I was going to make reference to the work that he's got going on, because this is a Government that's working hand in glove across our portfolios to make sure we support each other.

One of the last points in my statement was that we can't stop every major incident from happening when it comes to the weather. These weather conditions are—. The new normal is quite different to what the old past was and it's catching up with us very quickly. But the point about being able to adapt very quickly and prepare ourselves for these issues is critical. And also I think that one of the things that particularly passengers want is that they want to know when things are going to happen. Making sure that we keep people informed is of critical importance.

I'm glad you mentioned ports, because I've spent a lot of time in ports over recent months, and I too recognise the importance that they play. When I went to Ireland, what I found striking was the importance that Holyhead played to the Irish economy and therefore to the European economy of getting goods into Wales and through to the rest of the UK. Holyhead is the second biggest roll-on, roll-off port in the country. What we've seen is that the investment that's been made since the December 2024 report is about to come online. contributions.item_title_en: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Transport: Climate Adaptation and Resilience in Wales's Transport Network
contributions.text_english:
And thank you for the general support for this statement as well. I think this is the work—. This summer has been a remarkable summer. Things have changed, and I think even most people who were previously sceptical of climate change have seen the impacts of it all around us. I think people are seeing it in their day-to-day lives. Sometimes late to the party, lots of people, but, ultimately, that's been important.

I think your point about the whole-system approach is really important. We've got the regional transport funds as well that have started on their process at the moment. Part of that is about making sure that they build resilience into their funding bids. I'll just reflect on Elyn Stephens's point in the last debate about getting over the Bwlch to get into the hospitals, and these are real issues that are part of this whole resilience package.

Now, the strategic road networks aren't in those such vulnerable positions as some of the roads that are in the control of the local authorities. So, there is partnership working between the local authorities. I referenced it in my statement, and that's been heightened by the fact that the need to be able to solve things, whether it's education or health, is really critical to this. So, I'm looking for much improved regional transport plans that look at the strategic impact of making sure our roads are accessible over winter and summer, because the strategic road network is impacted by heat waves as well as by winter. Winter seems more acute, especially as we're going into it now.

I'm really pleased you mentioned bus. I did reference bus in the statement, but bus is the key way that people get across our country via public transport. It's used by many more people than the rail service is and it's often, at times, forgotten. Buses were affected in this heat wave this summer. There were bus services that were drawn from operation because they were too hot for the driver to operate and also for the passengers in there as well. And I think the lessons learned from this are actually about moving ahead.

You've mentioned bus franchising. A part of that is about a bus renewal plan, so the new fleet we need, the fleets for the future, and we've got lots of those. You've seen them. If you're around our capital city, you will have seen electric buses that have got air conditioning. They work really well. And we've got other places around Wales that are still using diesel buses without air conditioning. So, there is a plan to move all buses into that. But there's also some simple stuff we can do. When we paint a roof of a bus white instead of black, it makes a real difference. The Taith Cymru coaches, which we're launching in two weeks' time, have all got white roofs. White roofs take about 4 degrees out of the temperature of the cab. Now, that cab is air conditioned, but the fact you can therefore make the whole system work better and the engines work better without having to cool the cab is really important. So, there's some really simple stuff we can do as well.

I apologise if I didn't say enough about the passenger. I think the passenger is central to this and I mentioned it in my answer to Jason a few minutes ago as well. Part of this is about being clear about our communication. There will be things that we can't address. There will be services that will have to stop where it's unsafe, because safety is the critical thing. But I think one of the things that we're getting a lot better at is understanding the forecasts that come in, preparing for them and being able to inform customers. Because part of what we all, I think, want is an integrated transport system. So, it's all very well if you can catch the bus to the train station, but if the train's not running, what's the point of catching the bus? So, I think that integration of message is absolutely key.

Your last point about joined-up thinking, and especially linking into other things that are going on—. The farmers who are doing some work that positively impacts the rail network underneath—I referenced the climate and nature action plan. That isn't my responsibility, it's a cross-Government responsibility. So, feeding into that can make a real difference, and a tangible difference to our rail and other transport infrastructure as well. So, it's a really good point. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Janet. I always welcome your contributions. I think that, in all seriousness, your real-life experience—. I remember when you and Tom were stuck and Tom—. So, these things do happen. I think that the interesting thing, for the purposes of this, is that we're talking about how we can manage better with issues of, particularly, extreme weather. But I think your points about the fact that, sometimes, other issues exacerbate some of those problems is worth noting into it as well.

I think we do have your support for the devolution of rail, but you mentioned the point about—[Interruption.] We'll try. You mentioned the point about points failures, and these are Network Rail's points, in the main, especially the routes that you're taking. So, the responsibility for those railways is being managed elsewhere. Now, I'm not denigrating the fact that they're working hard to do some of these things, but we're not the priority in some of these changes. So, I think one of the things that this talks to is the fact that we want to take responsibility for us. And the improvement in the services on the core Valleys lines—when we've got the whole service; we've got the track, the train and everything else—is marked and it's been marked and it's improving month on month. I think that talks to what sort of rail system we could have in the future. I'm really pleased that you talked about how disruption affects the most vulnerable first, and I think that's, again, something that links back to the conversation with Vikki and with Jason about making sure that our communication is really clear, particularly to those people who may not be able to find that the journey—. It's already a challenge, the journey that we've got. And part of that, I think, talks to us about making sure that we communicate in a way that's most effective for the people who are taking the journey as well—that's really critical for it.

I just think the last—. Just in terms of passengers requiring accurate information, I think that that is also something that—. I feel that this young guy who you were talking to who missed his job appointment as well, some of that is about—. And again, I'm linking it to how do we make sure that, particularly in extreme weather conditions, we get these things right so that communications are clear as we go through.

The last point: at the start of this I made a commitment to make a statement on the north Wales main line changes, that was obviously a Network Rail decision to close that main line. The communication around that initially was really poor—we found out by accident rather than by design. But, because we found out early enough, we can get in there and make sure that we've got these bus replacement services that do their best to be able to pick up the slack. Now this isn't the way that you'd want to go and plan it, because everyone in the north of the country now must be dreading what's going to happen in January, including Members in this room as well, so I understand that. What I can do, as transport Minister, is make sure that, where we've got those rail replacement services, they run regularly, they're good services, they're also services that can hit the timetables that we were hitting before. So, hopefully, disruption will be kept to a minimum, because we've got a bit more time to plan for this than we should have had. But, ultimately, this was a decision that was made without our say-so, and it was made to us, not with us.

contributions.item_title_en: 10. Short Debate: The importance of port infrastructure and maritime traffic to the Welsh economy
contributions.text_english:
You're probably not going to realise how much I actually like ports, but you'll find out after this, because I've got quite a lot I want to say. I'm sure you'd like to go home, but there's a lot in ports. Wales is home to a strong and diverse ports and maritime sector, comprising businesses that consistently demonstrate resilience, innovation and adaptability. Their contribution is fundamental to our economic success, facilitating the movement of vital imports and exports, supporting key industries and providing rewarding careers for thousands of people across our coastal communities.

The most recent recorded data from the British Ports Association suggests Welsh ports account for approximately 1.2 per cent of Welsh gross value added, about £560 million, and support almost 11,000 jobs. We recognise the immense value these businesses bring to Wales. While much of their work takes place behind the scenes, it is vital to our daily lives and to the smooth functioning of our economy.

As a nation with an extensive coastline, deep water access and a strategic position between Ireland and key international shipping routes, Wales has long relied upon its ports to support trade, investment and economic growth. Today, that role is more important than ever. Perhaps the greatest opportunity for our ports is the transition to clean energy and the growth of offshore renewables. Wales offers many very attractive propositions to the offshore wind sector. For example, in Port Talbot, ABP are completing the essential design and engineering work needed to build one of the first floating offshore wind ports in the UK. This new development will help unlock an initial 4.5 GW of floating offshore wind projects in the Celtic sea, enough to power 6.5 million homes.

Another example is Erebus, a proposed floating wind development off the Pembrokeshire coastline. Its significance is not only the turbines offshore, but what comes with them onshore, both in terms of supply chain opportunities and the infrastructure needed to support new offshore industries, such as fabrication, logistics, marine services and long-term maintenance work. In the north, the Awel y Môr offshore windfarm off the coast of the north of Wales is now moving towards construction, and a final investment decision. It will be developed by RWE on behalf of project partners for an area of sea bed to the west of the existing Gwynt y Môr offshore windfarm. Once completed, it will generate power equivalent to the needs of more than half of Wales's homes, as well as creating opportunities throughout its construction, operational and eventual decommissioning process.

The Morlais tidal stream energy project manages an area of 35 sq km off the sea bed near Ynys Cybi on Anglesey. The scheme has the potential to generate up to 240 MW of low-carbon clean electricity, and provides further economic opportunities for operations and maintenance of our Welsh ports. The port of Mostyn, a privately owned and operated port in the north of Wales, has been leading the way for fixed offshore wind development, with around 240 people directly employed servicing the offshore wind sector.

We will continue to support ports to maximise the opportunities off the coast of the north of Wales and in the Irish sea, at least 7.6 GW with Gwynt y Môr and Mona projects in Welsh seas. contributions.item_title_en: 10. Short Debate: The importance of port infrastructure and maritime traffic to the Welsh economy
contributions.text_english:
Alongside supporting renewable energy generation, the maritime sector itself is undergoing significant transformation as it moves towards decarbonisation. Ports will play a crucial role in enabling the adoption of alternative fuels, supporting cleaner vessel technologies and developing the infrastructure required for low-carbon shipping, and supporting the decarbonisation of transport. This transition presents both challenges and opportunities, creating the potential for innovation, investment and new high-skilled employment across Wales.

Maritime traffic remains fundamental to Wales's trading relationships, particularly with Ireland, one of our most important trading partners. The port of Holyhead is—I repeat my line from earlier—the second busiest roll-on, roll-off ferry port in the UK and it is a vital gateway into Wales. In recognition of this, a £150 million scheme is in place to secure the port's long-term future through the refurbishment of its essential and historic breakwater.

Holyhead and our other major west coast ferry ports, Fishguard and Pembroke Dock, provide vital international connectivity for goods and people. Despite the adverse impacts of Brexit on the volume of freight using the UK's land bridge between Ireland and the rest of the EU, these ports remain essential to the UK and Irish logistics sector. The economic importance of these Irish sea links were highlighted in December 2024, with the prolonged disruption at Holyhead having a significant impact on businesses on both sides of the water. In response to this, the Irish sea taskforce was created to examine what could be done to avoid a repeat scenario and respond effectively if similar events ever happened again at any Welsh port. I intend to publish a six-month update to the Irish sea taskforce recommendations this autumn.

Following this and other similar incidents, the Holyhead Port Authority, Stena Line, has committed to a multi-million pound port infrastructure investment in the berths to strengthen the long-term resilience of this port and modernise its infrastructure for the future. Separately, Stena Line has invested a further £20 million into a new linkspan at Fishguard port, which will strengthen future resilience and connectivity and enhance opportunities for them to increase their roll-on, roll-off traffic and expand their cruise ship offering at the port.

Cruise tourism plays a significant role in our maritime economy and, for many visitors, our ports provide their first welcome to Wales. Cruise Wales is a partnership between Welsh Government, our six cruise ports, Welsh tourist destinations and many outside stakeholders. We market six cruise ports in Wales, which are Cardiff, Swansea, Pembroke, Milford Haven, Fishguard and Holyhead. Cruise Wales is an established global brand attracting new cruise lines to Wales. Our ports continue to support a thriving cruise sector. In 2026, 88 cruise calls are scheduled at Welsh ports, bringing over 73,500 passengers and 35,000 crew. This is expected to generate circa £7.6 million in visitor spending, providing a valuable boost to local economies across Wales.

Our ports are not simply points of arrival and departure. They are centres of economic activity that support investment, innovation and employment across Wales. Welsh ports have the potential to attract significant investment, stimulate innovation, strengthen strategic industries and create high-quality employment opportunities across Wales.

Another example of how important port infrastructure is to our economy is the recently agreed long-term lease and commercial agreement between Associated British Ports and Valero at the port of Cardiff, securing critical supply and storage solutions for liquid fuels across south Wales. The agreement underpins the ongoing operation of Valero's 12-acre liquid fuels terminal at Roath Dock, the largest such facility at the port of Cardiff, and represents a commitment to the future of the port and the Wales energy supply chain. The deal safeguards skilled jobs on site and supports the reliable supply of fuel for households, businesses, airports and commercial fleets across the south of the country. It also takes thousands of HGVs off the road network by using coastal shipping routes to link Cardiff to Valero's Pembroke refinery at Milford Haven, the UK's leading energy port.

contributions.text_english:
Since taking office—I almost said 'leaving office' then; that would have been good. [Laughter.] Since taking office, I have visited—[Interruption.] Don't start. [Laughter.] I have visited many of our ports to see first-hand the essential role they play in supporting trade, industry and local communities. Whether handling passengers, facilitating freight movements, supporting steel production, construction projects, agriculture or manufacturing, our ports form an integral part of the supply chains that underpin the Welsh economy. It's been fascinating to observe how modern ports operate with such precision, co-ordinating the movement of vessels, cargo and people in a highly complex movement. I was on the bridge of a ferry that docked in Rosslare and I was able to witness the captain be able to berth the ship within six inches of its desired place. This is incredible precision and incredible skill.

Welsh ports have a rich sense of history—sorry, I'm going to go to the history now, I've got to go to it—have a rich sense of history and a social and cultural connection to their local communities and surrounding hinterland. I had the pleasure of learning about the connection ports have to their communities during my visit to Fishguard and Rosslare, where they were celebrating the first sea crossing from Fishguard to Rosslare that took place on 30 August 1906. This year marks the hundred and twentieth anniversary of this vital link between Ireland and Wales, connecting generations of families, holidaymakers, businesses and communities on both sides of the Irish sea. It was in 1906 that a newly built harbour and railway opened in Abergwaun, which also brought transatlantic liners to the port, and is still from where Stena Line runs its passenger service to Rosslare.

In 1807, Captain John Macgregor Skinner astonished mariners by successfully bringing his ship into Holyhead harbour during an exceptionally severe gale. Little of the current harbour infrastructure, including the sheltering breakwater, existed back then. Captain Skinner had to navigate rough waters and pass numerous rocks and small islands. This continues today, as every operation is carefully managed to ensure goods and services move safely, efficiently and on time, maximising economic value and supporting businesses across Wales and beyond.

I recently toured Rosslare port's impressive operations, which are completely different to those that were in place 126 years ago. Rosslare Europort is today a key infrastructure hub for transportation from Ireland to Europe and the UK. Post Brexit, Rosslare has experienced significant growth, particularly in freight traffic and direct ferry services to Europe. Weekly sailings to Europe increased more than sixfold. Welsh ports were not so fortunate. Holyhead and Fishguard ports saw a 30 per cent drop in traffic in 2021, according to their operator, Stena Line.

When in Ireland, I met with one of Ireland's leading temperature-controlled logistics companies to better understand their operations and experiences of using the Irish sea crossing between Dublin and Holyhead. We discussed the location of Welsh truck stops for driver welfare across the A55 corridor and how we could best support drivers to use alternative routes across Wales should their usual route not be open. This was followed by a meeting with my counterpart in the Irish Government, Seán Canney. Our discussions focused on strengthening resilience, deepening co-operation, and building the strong relationships necessary to support this vital maritime corridor.

These partnerships ensure that, when challenges arise, we can engage rapidly and work collaboratively to deliver effective solutions. I've also—and this talks directly to the point about resilience—asked officials to prepare an internal resilience exercise over the coming months, with key stakeholders on both sides of the Irish sea, focusing on scenario planning in the event of an unforeseen Welsh port closure.

The contribution made by Welsh ports in maritime traffic cannot be overstated. They enable trade, support critical supply chains, attract investment, strengthen energy security, create skilled employment, and connect Wales with key international markets. They are essential to our economic prosperity today and will be equally important in helping us to achieve our ambitions for a greener and more resilient economy in the future. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

contributions.text_english: Dirprwy Lywydd, today I would like to set out the next steps for the Menai crossings and the M4 around Newport. We have agreed a way forward.
contributions.text_original: Dirprwy Lywydd, heddiw hoffwn nodi’r camau nesaf ar gyfer croesfannau'r Fenai a’r M4 o amgylch Casnewydd. Rydym wedi cytuno ar y ffordd ymlaen.

contributions.item_title_en: 4. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Transport: Strategic Priorities for the Menai Strait Crossings and M4 around Newport
contributions.text_english:
The challenges on these routes are not new. They affect communities, businesses and travellers every day. The reviews we commissioned at the start of the summer were not about repeating decades of work explaining the problems, they were intended to identify a practical way forward. They have given us a clear direction. Today I am announcing action to develop a third Menai crossing and action to develop roads-based and engineering solutions for the M4 around Newport, alongside a programme of improvements that will help people and businesses while that work progresses.

Dirprwy Lywydd, people on Ynys Môn and across the north of our country know how disruptive it can be when one of the Menai crossings is restricted or closed. The review confirms that resilience remains the key challenge. That is why this Government will immediately recommence development work for a third Menai crossing. This will include design development, environmental assessment, business case preparation and the statutory processes needed to establish a deliverable scheme.

People have waited a long time for certainty about the future of the crossings. Today we are providing that direction. A third crossing remains the most effective option for improving resilience and providing additional capacity across the Menai strait. But major infrastructure cannot be delivered simply by announcing it. The necessary development work must be undertaken if we are to move from aspiration to a proposal that, ultimately, can be developed.

Alongside this work, we will continue investing in the infrastructure that we already have. We will maintain and operate both existing crossings to keep them safe and reliable. We will continue investment in targeted resilience measures on Britannia bridge, including wind deflectors, variable speed limits and other operational improvements designed to reduce disruption and keep traffic moving during challenging conditions. These measures will not replace the need for a third crossing. They will help improve resilience while development work on the third crossing progresses.

The review also examined three-lane tidal flow operation on Britannia bridge. The evidence identified significant safety and operational concerns and does not support taking this option forward.

Dirprwy Lywydd, turning now to the M4 around Newport: this is one of the most important transport corridors in Wales. Every day, thousands of people and businesses rely on this route to get to work, move goods and connect with customers, communities and ports across Wales. Yet, congestion continues to cause unreliable journeys and disruption that can quickly spread across the wider network. The review is clear that doing nothing is not an option. It also shows there is no single short-term intervention capable of solving the problem on its own. That is why this Welsh Government will now begin an 18-month programme of work to develop roads-based and engineering solutions for the M4 around Newport. This programme will consider a range of roads-based and engineering interventions and will identify a preferred option capable of providing a long-term response to the challenges on this route.

contributions.item_title_en: 4. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Transport: Strategic Priorities for the Menai Strait Crossings and M4 around Newport
contributions.text_english:
Many people will understandably say that this issue has been debated for decades. They are right. But this work is not about revisiting old arguments. It is about developing options against current policy, environmental requirements, planning considerations and future travel demands, so that decisions can be taken on the basis of robust evidence and a clear understanding of what can realistically be delivered. Our objective is straightforward: we need a solution that is affordable, deliverable and capable of attracting the support and investment needed to make it happen. Without undertaking this work, there can be no credible pathway towards delivering future roads-based and engineering solutions.

But while this work progresses, we cannot simply wait. That is why we are also announcing a programme of improvements over the next five years. We will invest in the maintenance and renewal of the existing motorway and strategic road network. Over many years, Governments have often faced a choice between accepting disruption now or delaying important work until later. Understandably, there has often been a desire to minimise disruption in the short term, but that can make long-term challenges harder to address. Key infrastructure now requires significant renewal and maintenance work. I want to be honest: there will be periods of disruption while this work takes place. Nobody wants roadworks. Nobody enjoys delays. But continuing to defer this work will only lead to greater disruption and cost in the future. This Government is choosing to deal with that problem now.

We will also implement a five-year delivery plan, focused on practical improvements that people will start to see over the next two to three years, with further benefits building over time. This will include improvements to the way the motorway is operated and managed, including targeted improvements to roads and junctions, including potential closures, in and around Newport to improve traffic flow and resilience. The review found that measures such as these offer some of the quickest opportunities to improve traffic flow and resilience in the M4.

But we also recognise that changes affecting the motorway can have consequences for local roads. We will therefore work closely with Newport City Council, local communities and Members to develop these interventions so that the local impacts are properly considered alongside the benefits to the M4. At the same time, we will introduce measures to improve freight resilience by making better use of alternative routes such as the A465. This will maximise the investment made in the A465, supporting the provision of facilities that HGV drivers deserve, and at the same time alleviating pressure on the M4.

We will also continue investing in public transport, making it easier for more people to choose rail and bus services for everyday journeys between Newport and Cardiff, across the wider M4 corridor, and onwards into the rest of Wales and into England. The UK Government has committed to funding the rail stations recommended by the South East Wales Transport Commission. Last week I attended the joint UK-Welsh Government Wales rail board to discuss how we can accelerate delivery. I am pleased that Network Rail have committed to work collaboratively with Transport for Wales to draw on the expertise of both organisations, and TfW will take a direct role in constructing the stations.

We are setting up a new network south-east Wales board to oversee delivery. I have asked the team to prioritise delivery of the Cardiff parkway and Magor and Undy stations, so that communities can begin to benefit from these investments as soon as possible. We will also seek to improve access to Severn Tunnel Junction railway station and support improvements to bus connectivity between Newport and Cardiff, giving real options for travellers.

Dirprwy Lywydd, for too long, people and businesses have seen congestion around Newport become an accepted part of everyday life. This Government is choosing to act. The programme we are taking forward could reduce peak-hour traffic by about one in 10 vehicles. On a motorway that is already operating at or above capacity at the busiest times, that matters. It is a meaningful improvement over doing nothing and simply accepting increasing congestion on the network. But what matters is what these improvements mean in practice for people using the network every day. It means better travel choices through improved rail and bus services. It means the network is better able to cope when incidents occur, reducing the risk of small problems becoming major disruption. These are practical improvements that people should begin to notice in their everyday lives over the coming years.

Dirprwy Lywydd, people want action, not endless discussion. They want government to deal with today's challenges while properly planning for the future. That is exactly what we are doing. At the Menai strait, we are getting on with the work needed to develop a third crossing whilst managing resilience now. Around Newport, we are developing long-term road space and engineering solutions for the M4 whilst delivering practical improvements over the next five years. These are major transport challenges that have built up over many years; they will not be resolved overnight. But, today, we are providing a clear direction, taking practical actions now and developing the longer-term solutions needed for the future.

Thank you for the question. Before I answer, I just want to thank those Members who turned up for the briefing with officials this morning, and also subsequent conversations in this regard. It was a shame that Members from Reform chose not to undertake those conversations. There were specific conversations that were not entered into, and that was a real shame, because that would have given them the chance to have understood some of the detail behind this more clearly.

In answer to the questions on Menai, I don't think the Member, frankly, understands the process you need to go through to build. This is a significant piece of engineering. It is appropriate that we do it in the phases that we say we are. To be clear, this Government is committed to delivering a third crossing across the Menai. There are no ifs, no buts. That is absolutely clear. What you have to do to do that is to take stages. Now, the Member, and all of this group around here, just seem to think that you can click a finger and things happen. Let's get into the real world. The real world is that it takes real work to get these things done. The interesting thing is, when I was speaking to civil servants earlier prior to this, I was saying I was looking forward to this debate, because I do look forward to these debates. Do you know what they were saying? They're looking forward to getting stuck in to doing the work. That's what they're waiting for, and that's what's going to happen. What's happened for too long is this body politic has failed to deliver. If we have conversations that are in the style that we've had today, we'll continue to do that. But the rest of the Siambr, hopefully, will focus on getting things done. Because if you're just going to backbite on that, it helps nobody, frankly.

Turning to the M4, I think this is a real misunderstanding as well of what a 10 per cent change will do on the M4 with the plan of action that we've put together. Ten per cent—. And I'm sure that Members opposite me as well are probably thinking, 'I wish we'd done some more of this 10 per cent.' But, over the past 27 years, there's been very limited change on the M4. This Government is committing itself, over the next five years, to making an actual difference to people. And 3 per cent here and 1 per cent there makes a real difference. This is about a strategic suite of projects that need to be deployed together. These are the ways that we make the difference to the M4. And it's not straightforward. There is no silver bullet. If there was, we'd talk about it. You talk about the black route as if it's deliverable. That went when it was cancelled. The protected route status went when it was cancelled. So, we're talking about decades of work to even get that off the ground. So, to suggest to the people outside that you can deliver it in an instant is disingenuous—and I'm being kind in saying that.

But the haulage companies are looking for facilities, because, unlike some parts of Europe where they actually invest in facilities for drivers—. Drivers are professional. Across the UK, we have very, very poor facilities. This Government is going to make a difference to that, and we've had support from across the industry to say that they want to see those facilities. That will direct people across the piece, and that's including people from Ireland as well as haulage companies from the UK.

Rail adding choice and taking people off the motorway—. One of the things about adding choice using rail is exactly what you just said, it takes people—. So, I may be taking a car; I can now use the rail. That frees up space on the motorway for those people who need to use the motorway in the way that you described. It's a practical way of making a difference. The sad thing is that the Burns review—. I can just hear muttering behind me. Do you want to make an intervention or not?

I referenced in my statement that Transport for Wales would be working on developing those stations. And, again, thank you for the constructive way you approached the conversation this morning. I do appreciate it. And I think the frankness—. I didn't expect agreements as you walked into the Siambr today to talk about this, but I think what we got was a situation of understanding some of the issues that we're addressing.

I think, when we talk about junction closures, the thing that I'm really clear about is that it's something where I do recognise the concerns that are out there, and this is something that is very, very important that we get right. So, as I said in my answer to Vikki just a few minutes ago, I'm committed to engaging not just with Newport City Council and the surrounding councils, but with traders and local communities to make sure we understand how things can be mitigated and how things can work better as well. The three junctions you're talking about, one of them is a full closure, whereas the other ones will see changes that are less severe. So, it's about understanding the impacts of each one, which will be quite different.

The other thing I think is important to note is that we talk about this as if the intra-Newport system is working well, and, frankly, it isn't. Whereas I've got responsibility for the strategic road network, this is about working with Newport City Council, together, and the corporate joint committee as well, to make sure that we're delivering across the piece to improve the whole thing. The M4 is part of the system that makes Newport work, or not at the moment, and we've got to improve that. It's a youthful city, and people are expecting a modern city with modern public transport facilities. But at the moment, today, it's the most car-dependent city in Wales. So, we've got to do things to give people the choice. And going back to the point I made earlier, that choice needs to be very real and needs to be effective.

On the A465, we've had discussions with hauliers; we'll have more discussions with hauliers. But the initial points were to be welcomed, particularly about the routes that we're talking about from Fishguard into the midlands. It's a perfect route for that, but currently, it's not being chosen as the route of choice, and part of that is about providing the facilities. At the moment, we have freight drivers who are having to park in car parks and lay-bys, and it's wholly inappropriate. This is something that we can make a definite difference on and can attract drivers onto that route again. And again, going back to every time we take some of that traffic off the M4, it frees up space for people who have no choice but to use the M4.

Tunnel widening was one of the points that was considered in this review. I would imagine that it'll be considered within the 18-month review as well, with more detail. But at this point in time, it was considered it wasn't something where we had a route to take forward at the moment. The timescales associated with the disruption are something like 12 years before it gets finished. So, it's something that we'll look at in more detail. And on that point, I'd encourage Members from across the piece to engage in that piece of work, to make sure that they find out what's going on, and I'll do my best to make sure that Members are appraised of it, as we go through.

In terms of the Menai and when it happens, there is a process that you need to go through to be able to get a bridge to start. We're making a commitment that we want this bridge to be built. I think I've made that clear. That process starts today. That process then goes through—. There are a number of stages to it. What I'll be doing is updating this Siambr with written statements to talk about how that progress happens. The major work on a bridge build happens in the latter end of that, after all the plans have been approved, and all the environmental regulations, et cetera, have been agreed to. So, you'll see the actual spades in the ground, but the real work, and a lot of the work, will start now. That work starts now. So, we're looking at somewhere between eight and 10 years for that bridge to be finished and to be opened. That's a realistic timetable. And as I hope Members will understand, I'd rather deal with realism, rather than deal with things that won't happen, which brings me to the black route.

This is a project now—. There is no deliverable opportunity for the black route. So, I would encourage the Members opposite, and other Members in the Siambr, just to think about what we can do to make practical improvements today. Because my concern is—and I've said this before—the body politic has let people down in Newport, and outside, by not solving these issues. So, there are lots of things you agree with, and I'm glad for that support.

contributions.item_title_en: 8. Short Debate: Congestion isn't inevitable: How the Welsh Government and Cardiff Council can improve the lives of motorists in Cardiff and the surrounding regions
contributions.text_english:
This debate starts with a very straightforward question: how do we make journeys better? The motion quite rightly focuses on motorists in Cardiff and the surrounding region, and I think we should take that seriously. I take that seriously. Congestion is one of those issues that almost everyone has experienced. It affects commuters travelling to work, businesses making deliveries, parents taking their children to school and people attending appointments. It can increase costs, reduce productivity and create frustration for those who simply want to get to where they need to be on time. But I think it is important that we are honest about the nature of the challenge.

Cardiff is a major centre for employment, public services and economic activity in the south-east of the country. It attracts significant numbers of people every day from surrounding areas and further afield. That success brings economic opportunities for Cardiff and the wider region, but it also places significant pressures on the transport network. Cars and roads remain a vital part of that network. Any serious transport strategy must recognise that reality. That is why the Welsh Government's approach is focusing on improving connectivity across the whole network.

For me, there are three realities we need to recognise. The first is that we need to make better use of the roads we already have. There are practical things that we can do: better management of incidents and roadworks, better information for drivers, making sure junctions and traffic signals operate as effectively as possible and understanding where the real constraints are so that we target investment where it can make a genuine difference. If there is a problem with a network, we should be prepared to tackle it. Roads matter. They carry people, goods, emergency services and businesses. They are not an optional extra in our transport system and we should not pretend that they are, and I don't pretend that they are.

But the second reality is that we cannot build our way out of congestion. There will always be a temptation to respond to congestion by adding more road capacity; we've heard a bit of that already. Sometimes that will be the right thing to do, but it is not automatically the right thing to do and we should be wary of assuming that more road space will, by itself, solve the problem. More road space can attract more traffic, and, if we respond to every increase in traffic with another road building project, we can find ourselves spending more and more without ever really getting ahead of the problem.

contributions.item_title_en: 8. Short Debate: Congestion isn't inevitable: How the Welsh Government and Cardiff Council can improve the lives of motorists in Cardiff and the surrounding regions
contributions.text_english:
This is not an argument against investment. It is an argument for being disciplined about where we invest, what we are trying to achieve, and whether the evidence tells us that an intervention will actually work. And that matters particularly when public money is under pressure. We have choices to make and we need to be able to explain why we are making them.

The third reality is probably the most important. If we want to make life better for motorists, which we do, we also need to make sure that not every journey is made by car. That may sound counterintuitive, but it isn't. If someone can make the journey by train, bus, bike or on foot, there is one less vehicle competing for the same limited road space. So, public transport is not anti-motorist. It is one of the ways we help the people who need to drive.

That is why the south Wales metro matters. It means better, more reliable and more frequent rail services between the Valleys and Cardiff. It is why our £70 million investment in Cardiff Central, and the new tramway between Cardiff Central and Cardiff Bay, matters. It's also why bus reform matters, and it is why bus priority, better interchanges, active travel and better regional connections all matter. Because giving people a genuine alternative to the car isn't about telling them what to do. It is about giving them a choice. Frankly, people are much more likely to leave the car at home when the alternative is good enough to make them want to.

This is the standard we should be aiming at: a bus that turns up, a train that people can rely on, a safe route to walk or cycle, and interchanges that actually work. A transport system that feels like one system, rather than a series of disconnected services. That's the ambition of one network, one timetable and one ticket. It is why regional planning actually matters. Because Cardiff's congestion is not simply a Cardiff problem. People travelling to Cardiff every day from Caerphilly, the Vale, Newport, Rhondda Cynon Taf, Bristol, and across the wider region, they don't stop being commuters when they cross the council boundary, and they certainly don't care which organisation is responsible for that particular stretch of road they are sitting on. They just want the journey to work.

So, our planning needs to reflect how people live and travel. The south-east Wales corporate joint committee provides an important framework for doing that. Because the transport network is a system. If we only look at individual roads, individual modes or individual local authority boundaries, we risk missing how the system actually behaves and how a problem in one place can quickly create a problem elsewhere.

That brings me to demand management. Cardiff Council is exploring the potential for a workplace parking levy. I recognise this is controversial, but I don't think it helps to reduce the debate to whether a workplace parking levy is simply good or bad. The proper questions are: what problem are we trying to solve? What would the intervention achieve? Who would pay? Who would benefit? What alternatives would people have? The current position is clear. There are no plans for the Welsh Government to bring forward the secondary legislation that would be required to enable a workplace parking levy in Wales. But I don't think that means we should stop thinking about the wider question. Our roads are under pressure, and we need to be willing to have an honest conversation about how we manage that pressure.

If proposals come forward in future, they would need to be evidence led, properly assessed, fair, and subject to the appropriate consultation and statutory processes. There is a simple principle I would apply: demand management should never be about making lives harder for the sake of it. If we ask people to change how they travel, we need to give them something better to travel on. That means better public transport, better active travel, better regional connectivity, and a road network that is properly managed for the people who still need to use it.

So, what would actually improve the lives of motorists? I think the answer is practical. It means more reliable journeys, fewer avoidable delays, better management of roadworks and incidents, and smarter use of the roads we already have. contributions.item_title_en: 5. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Transport: Our Vision for the Devolution of Rail
contributions.text_english:
Railways are more than steel tracks and timetables, they are the arteries of our nation, connecting people to jobs, to education, to family and opportunity. When our railways work well, Wales works well. When they fall short, communities and the nation’s prosperity are held back. The current system for our railways is fragmented. Infrastructure is largely controlled at a UK level. Unlike the Scottish Government, the Welsh Government has no control over rail infrastructure investment. Accountability is shared in respect of the services delivered jointly by the Welsh and UK Governments, but not the levers to drive change. That means that decisions affecting passengers in Wales are too often made elsewhere, without the full alignment of Welsh priorities.

For decades, the UK Government has failed to invest in the Welsh rail network and has instead allowed it to decline. The network in Wales makes up around 10 per cent of the total British network by track length, yet, over the past 15 years, Wales has received only 1.5 per cent of the total investment in enhancements. And starkly, only 9 per cent of the network is electrified, largely as a result of the core Valleys lines, compared to 45 per cent in England and 33 per cent in Scotland. And parties across the Siambr have acknowledged the unfairness of HS2 funding. We have lost out on consequential funding of £850 million up to the end of this spending review period, and that figure is growing exponentially now that the UK Government assesses that HS2 will now cost more than £100 billion. In comparison, the Scottish Government has received around £1.3 billion additional funding as a result of comparability with HS2, up to the end of the current spending review period. The Northern Ireland Executive has received around £0.5 billion. Our ambition is to change that. We have a vision of a devolved rail network, where rail services are designed around the needs of our people, our communities and our economy.

Transport for Wales has already demonstrated what would be possible if Wales was responsible for both track and train. Through the transformation of the core Valleys lines, they have demonstrated that Wales can successfully own, manage and deliver major rail infrastructure transformation, which will change the lives of people in the south of the country, through better connecting communities and making them a more attractive place for businesses to start and grow. Our vision is to see that replicated throughout Wales, developing Cardiff Crossrail to make it easier for people to travel sustainably through our capital; building new stations in the south west, through the Swansea bay and west Wales metro; increasing rail capacity in the north of Wales through network north Wales; and increasing capacity through the middle of the country on the Marches line. This would be transformational to connectivity in Wales, but it will only be possible to deliver in full with the right powers and funding.

Today, I want to set out the steps that we will take to move towards this vision, pursuing further devolution in a phased pragmatic way. Our first action will be to work constructively with the Department for Transport to deliver improvements under the current system. The UK Government recognised its historical lack of investment in Welsh railways in February and committed to funding Transport for Wales's £14 billion rail vision. Through the UK and Welsh Government Wales rail board, we will work constructively with them to agree priorities and a timeline for this funding and develop a credible pipeline of schemes, but we will also hold them to account to deliver on their promise for Wales.

The Wales rail board also provides an opportunity for us to press that the schemes announced in the 2025 spending review are delivered at pace in this spending review period that runs up to 2029-30. In particular, I'll be focusing on how we can accelerate delivery of the Burns stations to offer greater connectivity and alternatives to M4 travel, and I expect Network Rail to work closely with Transport for Wales so that we can deliver these stations as quickly as possible.

Secondly, the UK Government’s Railways Bill represents a significant moment of change, and we need to ensure the Bill works for Wales in a way consistent with our pathway to devolution. For the UK, it proposes a new public body, Great British Railways, to bring together track and train across Great Britain. It also introduces new mechanisms for collaboration between Governments, including a memorandum of understanding between the UK and Welsh Governments. But we must also be clear: the Bill does not fundamentally change where power sits; it does not provide Wales with control over rail infrastructure, its funding or investment decisions.

As currently drafted, I have serious concerns about how a number of the clauses in the Bill affect the role of Welsh Ministers and this Senedd. I have already set these out to the UK rail Minister, seeking further engagement on how our aspirations for rail can be safeguarded and furthered. He has committed to urgent discussions so that we can ensure the current reforms secure better outcomes for Wales.

To address these concerns, I will seek to ensure the Bill firstly enables a statutory underpinning for the role of Welsh Ministers and the MOU, enables parity for Transport for Wales and a deepening of the partnership with Great British Railways, and enables protection and enhancement of the devolved competence of the Senedd in respect of railways. These actions can improve how decisions are made, ensuring Wales has a stronger voice and clearer influence, making a difference to passengers.

Thirdly, our manifesto commits us to negotiating fairer rail funding for Wales, and this remains central to our approach. Later this afternoon, we will hear from the Prif Weinidog, setting out our priorities for fair funding, something that is felt egregiously when it comes to rail.

I have already written to the Secretary of State for Transport to set this out, and the Cabinet Minister for Finance will press for changes that recognise the reality of rail in Wales, including funding arrangements that reflect our responsibilities, recognition of Welsh Government ownership of infrastructure such as the core Valleys lines, and a fair share of investment to address historic underfunding. Without fair funding, devolution cannot succeed. With it, we can unlock transformational change.

Finally, we will make the case for full devolution for Wales. That means decisions over rail funding taken not in Westminster but in Wales, as is already the case in Scotland; track and train integrated in Wales, as UK Government are seeking to do in England, with infrastructure devolved to Wales along with services on the network; and for cross-border infrastructure and services, a partnership role for Wales with UK Government and GBR to deliver effective management. This would provide a step change in our ability to align investment with Welsh needs, whilst managing risk in a balanced way.

This Government wants to see a new Wales Bill to legislate for this and further powers for the Welsh Ministers, to give us the tools to improve the lives of people in Wales. I fully expect to work with UK Ministers to explore the pathway to achieving these objectives, whilst ensuring the Welsh rail network remains fully integrated with the wider GB rail network and continues to provide seamless connectivity.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you for the question, I think, Jason. We enjoyed our first conversation when we met to talk about these issues, and I hope to have more of those constructive conversations into the future, and perhaps we spend our time talking about transport, which is the job I'm paid to do, which I think would be easier for me to do.

You referenced whingeing. I'll tell you what I'm not doing. I'm not whingeing. I'm preparing to get on with the job to make Wales's transport system work, and rail is a key part of it. Now, when you speak to people about the proof of the pudding, the core Valleys lines and what's happened on the metro is a perfect example of what can happen when we get our act together and start working on it. And if you travel on it, you'll see the benefits of it, and you hear people every day saying how important it is that they can turn up to a station and get on a train that's comfortable and works and does the job it needs to do. We need to make that happen for the whole of Wales. Connectivity in some parts of Wales is really poor. Part of our responsibility is to make sure that changes. We cannot do that when people in Westminster are making the decisions and we have no say in it. We need to be the people making those decisions, and we have the proof that we can do it.

The key thing that matters for making things happen is making sure there's a supply chain. One of the things that I'm acutely aware of is that we've got people who've delivered the core Valleys lines, who've delivered the metro, and they're raring and willing to go on the next stage of our next project when it comes to Wales. We've got the plans for the Burns stations. We need to get them going. I had a constructive conversation with the UK Government. We're going to pursue that in the same way as I think we agreed we'd have constructive conversations as well, as I did with others around this Siambr. But one of the things we shouldn't do is start suggesting that this is whingeing. This is about getting on with it. This is what we're doing. This is what I'm keen to do, and I won't be whingeing at all.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Vikki. Thank you for the question. So, I'm not going to stand up here—and I think we made it clear when we met—to be churlish about the work that's going on, and I feel we're building on the good work that's happened so far with the core Valleys lines, with the metro. I think this is good work, but we need to push it further, and I think that what we're setting out here is an acceleration of that move to take things on. And this is why devolution becomes so important, because, ultimately, this is about us making sure that the decisions are made in the right place to effect the right things.

We don't think—and I think it's been broadly accepted previously in the Siambr—that Westminster's the right place to decide our rail infrastructure spending. The proof of the pudding is in a figure that I spoke about earlier: we've got 10 per cent of the rail network, yet only 1 per cent of the enhancements has been spent in Wales. So, we've been historically underfunded. Now, the £445 million that's in this spending review is a step in the right direction. It's insufficient to deliver the Burns stations in the way they need to be delivered. So, we're having a constructive conversation. And you asked about the specifics. I was really pleased with the positivity that came from my conversation with UK Government—pleasantly pleased with how it went. We've committed, the rail Minister and I, to also go into the next Wales rail board, where we can continue that engagement where the teams around us can see we're still on the same page.

You asked whether I stood steadfast behind Transport for Wales's vision, and I do. This is something that makes a clear difference to Wales. But the problem is it needs to be funded properly, and that's the critical thing. So, when we're talking about the £14 billion, which has been repeated, we need to see that laid out in the next spending review, so that we can get on and do the work. What I've found with Transport for Wales is that they're ready to get on and do it, so I want to give them the resources, through the Cabinet Minister for Finance, to help that become a reality. Because the people of Wales are fed up with people kicking the can down the road. I'm not going to do that. What I want to make sure is that we get some movement on it.

I welcome the question on devolution. I'm a big fan of devolution. I think that devolution is appropriate when it's at the right level. So, the key thing about devolution is making sure you make the right decisions at the right level. Rail, that's at a Wales level, and I'm clear about that. That's where we should be focused.

When it comes to other priorities, I think we're in the right place. I think we're in the place where the CJCs make those decisions through the regional transport funds. But I think where we've got to do some more work is making sure that the citizen understands how they can influence that process. So, today, I think constituents know how to contact me in Pen-y-bont Bro Morgannwg. They would have known how to contact me as a local councillor. I'm not sure that citizens know how to engage with the CJCs in the same way. So, I think, when it comes to devolution, you need to make sure there's that link to make sure that works as well. But, generally, thank you for your questions. I think they're all constructive, and I appreciate that level of challenge and scrutiny. Diolch.

I was really pleased with the positivity that came from my conversation with UK Government—pleasantly pleased with how it went. We've committed, the rail Minister and I, to also go into the next Wales rail board, where we can continue that engagement where the teams around us can see we're still on the same page.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you, Peter, and, again, thank you for the constructive way you've framed the questions, albeit there's a few things that I think we take slightly different views on. But if we start at your last point first, 'Is power the important thing or is making people's lives better the more important thing?' Do you know, if I could see a way of being able to deliver things without power then I'd investigate that first? My first two points in my statement reference working with UK Government more constructively with the current powers that we've got. So, I want to be clear, when I'm dealing with UK Government, that I'm going to be somebody who always works constructively, is always honest and tries to get the best out of that relationship. That includes where we're connected across the country, and making sure that those things work. So, I'm not somebody who's just, there, power for power's sake.

However, it is increasingly clear, if you just look—. You referenced the electrification figure. Only 9 per cent of our rail network is electrified; 45 per cent of the English network is electrified. The only reason, really, that 9 per cent is electrified isn't necessarily about GWR; it's more about what the Welsh Government did with regard to the core Valleys lines. So, let's make sure we get these things right before we move on.

I'm glad you brought up the issue of resilience. I think we need to look at this in the frame of where things are happening. So, just as a backward look, when we had the red weather warning 10 days ago, 94 per cent of Transport for Wales services ran appropriately. Now, if you compare that to Paris, Paris lost 10 per cent of its network in the same period. Germany lost every single train that doesn’t have air conditioning in it, which was a huge number of trains, and Belgium similarly. So, we’ve got to be careful that we don’t characterise our transport network incorrectly. That doesn’t mean that we don’t need to do a lot of work on making sure we’re resilient and ready for these things. We’re about to hit another heatwave now, so these things aren’t going away. This will be three heatwaves this year so far. So, I think this is a really important point, and I expect to come back to this Siambr in short order to be able to talk about how we build a more resilient network. Part of it is about making sure the trains we put on the network, the buses we put on our roads, are appropriate to deliver the services. So, I was on a bus the other day, fully air-conditioned, it makes it a comfortable journey, the trains are similarly so, and that makes a real difference to things as well.

We enjoyed our walk to school, I think, in Magor the other day, and it was good to see how committed the team were there to their project. The reflection I have from it is how long it's taken them to get to a point where progress happens, even in developing their community centre. And I think one of the things I'm keen to do is to make sure that we collectively can agree on lots of things. The more we can agree on, the more commitment people can start, and the funds can start to flow so that we know, even in four years' time, if the make-up of the Siambr changed in any way, we all know that we're committed to doing the things we are. And things like the Burns stations fit that profile. So, I welcome the broad support, I think, from you in this regard, and I think we'll continue to work together.

contributions.text_english:
We have made tangible progress that reflects both the ambition of this Government and the practical steps we are immediately taking to improve public transport for people and communities right across Wales.

For decades, our communities across much of Wales have faced real difficulty travelling between the north and the south, particularly in the west of the country. contributions.text_english:
Thank you for your question, Jason. I think what we've talked about there—. There are a lot of things that I would agree with in that statement and I think it's good to see that there's a lot of ambition that you want to see, and this is part of that.

I'll tell you what this starts as being is a pragmatic start to make sure that things work, because we can wait forever for things to change, or we can make a difference quickly. This is about making a difference quickly; it's about making a difference that we know people will want to use. And we know that people will be interested in this. When we went out and consulted about this, 60 per cent of those people who were in that consultation said that they wanted to see this service that we've set out here, so we're confident that this is going to work.

I think your point about it being operationally resilient is really important. And this is something that's at the heart of what we've set out here. This is the reason we've got these two-hour coaches. We want people to trust in them, we want people to believe that these are going to turn up when we say they're going to turn up, which is the reason we've limited the stops. We need to make sure that the coach can get from A to B, from north to south, in a time that's convenient for people and works for people. So, that's really important. It's also why we've already got eight coaches in the yard, ready to go.

You mentioned integration, and I think integration is probably one of the key points of this service. To make it work, it needs to integrate. I referenced ports in my statement, but also integration with different towns that aren't on the direct network. Transport for Wales have been programming this whole system in, so it becomes a whole-system approach. So, it links into smaller conurbations that are on the outside, and they fit in and they can make sure that they're part of this solution too.

Affordability is central to this, Dirprwy Lywydd, and I think that's one of the issues that we'll be talking to at the start. But the guarantee I can give is that this will be an affordable service that will make sense for people's pockets. It will be cheaper than a car, and it'll be the right service that people choose.

I like the fact that you support our rail network. I look forward to talking about rail devolution next week. I hope to get the support from you behind us when we talk about rail devolution to make sure that we can talk with a united voice to UK Ministers when that time comes.

I'll finish by saying the way that this project will be extended will be based on how it gets used. We are confident that we can deliver the service as it is now, but that doesn't mean we don't add stops in the future. That would be something that we'd look at on a demand-led basis. But the demand as it stands at the moment is what we've got here. Diolch.
